subject: Business
title: Sunk Cost Fallacy
description: A fast breakdown of Sunk Cost Fallacy for builders.

hook.text: You paid $200 for concert tickets. It's raining. You're sick. You go anyway because you already paid.

buildup.text: The sunk cost fallacy means letting past spending influence future decisions it shouldn't affect.

discovery.text: Rationally, the money is gone either way. The only question is: will going make you happy now?

twist.text: Companies do this at massive scale. Projects get more funding because they've already spent millions.

climax.text: The Concorde jet kept flying for decades at a loss because governments wouldn't admit the investment failed.

punchline.text: What you've already spent shouldn't decide what you do next.

quiz.question: Why is the Concorde jet an example of sunk cost fallacy?
options: Governments kept funding it because of prior investment, not future viability
It was a profitable project that was cancelled too early
It was the fastest commercial plane ever built

details.summary: The sunk cost fallacy drives people to continue investing in failing projects because of what they have already spent rather than evaluating future prospects objectively. Rationally, past costs are irrelevant to forward-looking decisions, but emotionally they feel impossible to waste.
details.whyItMatters: Sunk cost thinking wastes billions in business each year through continued investment in failing projects, products, and strategies. Recognizing this fallacy is essential for making rational resource allocation decisions.
takeaways: Past expenditures should not influence decisions about future investment
Emotional attachment to prior investment distorts rational evaluation
Kill criteria set before projects begin help overcome sunk cost bias

faq.question: Why is it so hard to abandon a project you invested heavily in?
faq.answer: Loss aversion makes abandonment feel like confirming a loss. Admitting failure threatens ego and reputation. Organizations create momentum that resists reversal. The Concorde effect describes how governments continued funding the supersonic jet despite clear commercial failure.

faq.question: How can organizations overcome sunk cost bias in project decisions?
faq.answer: Establish clear kill criteria and review gates before projects begin. Use independent reviewers who lack emotional attachment. Ask whether you would start this project today knowing what you know now. Celebrate smart kills alongside successful launches.
